records.text: Take your antibiotic the way it was prescribed. It helps prevent infection.
Take your pain medicine the way it was prescribed. Take it before the pain gets bad.
Two days after surgery, remove the mastoid dressing, or head bandage. Next, check whether tape covers the incision, or surgical cut, behind the ear.

If there is tape, keep the area dry until three days after surgery. Do not clean the incision before that time. If there is no tape, clean the edges of the incision gently twice a day. Use a mix of equal parts hydrogen peroxide and distilled water. Then apply an over-the-counter antibiotic ointment, such as bacitracin.
Three days after surgery, you may shower and wash your hair. Your clinic will give you the date for your wound check and ear exam. The stitches dissolve, so they do not need to be removed.
Call your surgeon or clinic staff if all three signs below are present. The incision is red and swollen. It does not get better over the next one to two days. It hurts when touched.

Call if you have a fever above 101.5 degrees Fahrenheit. Call if the skin behind your ear is swollen or feels like fluid is building up under it. Call if you have a headache, light sensitivity, or excessive lethargy. Call if you have a wound-care question or another medical concern about you or your child.

For routine questions for the clinic or surgeon, leave a message on the nursing line at 415-353-2148. The UCSF page says you should get a call within 12 hours. If no one calls, call again. For an emergency, call 415-476-1000 and ask for the Otolaryngology resident on call.
After the surgery site has healed, you return for your first programming visit.
At the visit, a hearing specialist called an audiologist programs the speech processor you wear outside your ear. The program is made for your needs.
At later visits, the team checks the implant and equipment and measures how they are working. You will keep returning for checks and fine-tuning.
